ladders.name: h2
ladders.title: Hartree-Fock for H₂
intro: This page builds a Hartree-Fock program for the hydrogen molecule, H₂, in six steps, starting from a single Gaussian function. Each step is a complete program that runs. The last one prints the ground-state energy, −1.1167 hartree at a bond length of 1.4 bohr, the value Szabo and Ostlund work out by hand in Modern Quantum Chemistry.

rungs.title: One Gaussian, and the overlap of two
rungs.why: Every integral in the calculation is built from pairs of these; get one pair right first
notes: Quantum chemistry expands each orbital in Gaussians, $\phi(\mathbf r) = N e^{-\alpha |\mathbf r - \mathbf A|^2}$, for one reason: the product of two Gaussians on different centers is a third Gaussian on a point between them. Every integral below leans on that.

The overlap of two normalized s-Gaussians is closed-form: $S = N_a N_b\,(\pi/p)^{3/2}\,e^{-(ab/p)\,|\mathbf A - \mathbf B|^2}$ with $p = a + b$ and $N_a = (2a/\pi)^{3/4}$. Two checks pin it down: a function overlaps itself exactly once, and the overlap falls as the centers separate.
rungs.code:
pi = 3.141592653589793
def dist_sq(A, B) {
    "Squared euclidean distance between two 3-vectors."
    d0 = A[0] - B[0]
    d1 = A[1] - B[1]
    d2 = A[2] - B[2]
    return d0 * d0 + d1 * d1 + d2 * d2
}
def prim_overlap(a, A, b, B) {
    "Overlap (a A | b B) for two normalized primitive s-Gaussians."
    p = a + b
    r2 = dist_sq(A, B)
    K = exp(-a * b / p * r2)
    Na = pow(2.0 * a / pi, 0.75)
    Nb = pow(2.0 * b / pi, 0.75)
    return Na * Nb * pow(pi / p, 1.5) * K
}
origin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
bond = [0.0, 0.0, 1.4]
self_overlap = prim_overlap(0.5, origin, 0.5, origin)
apart = prim_overlap(0.5, origin, 0.5, bond)
show self_overlap
show apart
test "a normalized Gaussian overlaps itself exactly once" {
    assert_near(self_overlap, 1.0, 1.0e-14)
}
test "two Gaussians a bond length apart overlap less, by exp(-(ab/p) R^2)" {
    assert_near(apart, exp(-0.25 * 1.4 * 1.4), 1.0e-14)
}

rungs.program:
# rung 1. One Gaussian, and the overlap of two

pi = 3.141592653589793
def dist_sq(A, B) {
    "Squared euclidean distance between two 3-vectors."
    d0 = A[0] - B[0]
    d1 = A[1] - B[1]
    d2 = A[2] - B[2]
    return d0 * d0 + d1 * d1 + d2 * d2
}
def prim_overlap(a, A, b, B) {
    "Overlap (a A | b B) for two normalized primitive s-Gaussians."
    p = a + b
    r2 = dist_sq(A, B)
    K = exp(-a * b / p * r2)
    Na = pow(2.0 * a / pi, 0.75)
    Nb = pow(2.0 * b / pi, 0.75)
    return Na * Nb * pow(pi / p, 1.5) * K
}
origin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
bond = [0.0, 0.0, 1.4]
self_overlap = prim_overlap(0.5, origin, 0.5, origin)
apart = prim_overlap(0.5, origin, 0.5, bond)
show self_overlap
show apart
test "a normalized Gaussian overlaps itself exactly once" {
    assert_near(self_overlap, 1.0, 1.0e-14)
}
test "two Gaussians a bond length apart overlap less, by exp(-(ab/p) R^2)" {
    assert_near(apart, exp(-0.25 * 1.4 * 1.4), 1.0e-14)
}
rungs.titleHtml: One Gaussian, and the overlap of two
rungs.whyHtml: Every integral in the calculation is built from pairs of these; get one pair right first
notesHtml: Quantum chemistry expands each orbital in Gaussians, ϕ(r)=Ne−α∣r−A∣2, for one reason: the product of two Gaussians on different centers is a third Gaussian on a point between them. Every integral below leans on that.

The overlap of two normalized s-Gaussians is closed-form: S=Na​Nb​(π/p)3/2e−(ab/p)∣A−B∣2 with p=a+b and Na​=(2a/π)3/4. Two checks pin it down: a function overlaps itself exactly once, and the overlap falls as the centers separate.

rungs.title: The overlap matrix of H₂
rungs.why: A single Gaussian is a poor hydrogen 1s (wrong cusp, wrong tail); STO-3G fixes it with three
notes: STO-3G writes each hydrogen 1s as a fixed sum of three normalized primitives, $\chi = \sum_p d_p\,\phi_p$. An integral over contracted functions is then a double sum over primitive integrals, weighted by $d_p d_q$ -- nine terms for a pair of hydrogens.

Put one such function on each proton, 1.4 bohr apart, and the overlap matrix comes out with $S_{11} = 1$ (the contraction is normalized) and $S_{12} = 0.6593$, the first number in Szabo and Ostlund's worked example (Modern Quantum Chemistry, section 3.5.2).
`contracted_one_elec` takes a `kind` so that one loop can serve every one-electron operator. It knows only kind 0, the overlap, for now. The next two rungs each teach it one more kind.

rungs.title: Kinetic energy
rungs.why: The first operator: it needs nothing new but one formula, which makes it the right first edit
notes: For s-Gaussians the kinetic integral is the overlap times a polynomial: $T = \frac{ab}{p}\left(3 - \frac{2ab}{p}|\mathbf A - \mathbf B|^2\right) S$. So `prim_kinetic` calls `prim_overlap` rather than repeating it.
One function changes: `contracted_one_elec` learns kind 1, the kinetic energy.

rungs.title: Nuclear attraction
rungs.why: The electron-nucleus term is the first integral that is not elementary: it needs F0
notes: The Coulomb operator $1/|\mathbf r - \mathbf C|$ is not a Gaussian, but it is an integral over Gaussians, and that turns the attraction into $V = -\frac{2\pi}{p} Z_C N_a N_b\,e^{-(ab/p)|\mathbf A-\mathbf B|^2}\,F_0\!\left(p\,|\mathbf P - \mathbf C|^2\right)$, where $\mathbf P$ is the product center and $F_0(T) = \int_0^1 e^{-T t^2}\,dt$ is the Boys function.

$F_0$ is computed here by Simpson's rule -- slow, and it reads like the definition. It also has a closed form, $F_0(T) = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi/T}\,\mathrm{erf}\sqrt T$, which the test uses as an independent check: two routes to one number.
Szabo and Ostlund: $V^{1}_{11} = -1.2266$, and the core Hamiltonian $H_{11} = -1.1204$, $H_{12} = -0.9584$.

rungs.title: Electron repulsion
rungs.why: Everything so far is one electron in a fixed field; repulsion is what makes it a many-body problem
notes: $(\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma)$ is the repulsion between the charge clouds $\chi_\mu\chi_\nu$ and $\chi_\lambda\chi_\sigma$. Each cloud collapses to one Gaussian at its product center, and the two interact through the same Boys function as before, now at $\frac{pq}{p+q}|\mathbf P - \mathbf Q|^2$.
This rung adds two functions and changes none. The contracted integral is a four-fold sum -- 81 primitive integrals for each of the 16 elements, of which symmetry leaves only four distinct values.

rungs.title: The self-consistent field
rungs.why: The Fock operator depends on the orbitals it determines, so the equations are solved by iteration
notes: With every integral in hand, Hartree-Fock is linear algebra in a loop: build $F = H^{\rm core} + G(P)$ from the density, diagonalize it in an orthonormalized basis ($X = S^{-1/2}$), occupy the lowest orbital, form the new density, repeat.
For H2 in a minimal basis symmetry fixes the orbitals, so the loop converges at once -- which makes it a clean test of the machinery rather than of convergence.
Szabo and Ostlund: $E = -1.1167$ hartree at $R = 1.4$ bohr, with orbital energies $\varepsilon_1 = -0.578$ and $\varepsilon_2 = +0.670$.
